primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Heterozygous pathogenic THRB variants commonly produce a dominant-negative thyroid hormone receptor beta with reduced transcriptional response to T3. Resistance within the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis blunts normal negative feedback, so free T4/T3 are elevated while TSH remains inappropriately normal or elevated.
vignette: A 24-year-old woman is referred after repeated laboratory testing shows elevated free thyroxine and triiodothyronine concentrations with a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration in the normal range. She has a small diffuse goiter but no tremor, weight loss, or heat intolerance. Her father and older sister have had similar thyroid test results without treatment. Repeat testing with a different assay gives the same pattern, and pituitary MRI is normal.
lead: Which molecular abnormality most likely explains this patient’s laboratory findings?
correct: A dominant-negative defect in thyroid hormone receptor beta that reduces T3-mediated transcriptional feedback
distractors: A gain-of-function mutation in the TSH receptor causing ligand-independent thyroid hormone synthesis
An autonomously functioning pituitary thyrotroph adenoma that secretes TSH despite elevated thyroid hormone levels
Increased thyroxine-binding globulin production that raises protein-bound thyroid hormone without increasing free hormone
Loss of thyroid peroxidase activity that prevents iodide organification and thyroid hormone synthesis
distractor_notes: Activating TSH-receptor signaling causes autonomous hyperthyroidism with suppression of pituitary TSH, unlike the repeatedly nonsuppressed TSH in this family.

A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma can also produce high free T4/T3 with nonsuppressed TSH, but a normal pituitary MRI plus an autosomal-dominant family pattern across generations strongly supports inherited RTHβ instead.
Increased TBG elevates total T4/T3 while free hormone and TSH are generally normal; the vignette specifies repeatedly elevated free hormone concentrations.
Thyroid peroxidase loss impairs thyroid hormone synthesis and causes hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, the opposite biochemical pattern.
key_expl: This pattern is resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ). Pathogenic THRB variants reduce tissue responsiveness to thyroid hormone and commonly act in a dominant-negative fashion. Because TRβ is important in hypothalamic and pituitary feedback, elevated circulating T4 and T3 fail to suppress TSH appropriately. Patients can be clinically near-euthyroid because thyroid hormone sensitivity varies among tissues. A familial pattern with persistently high free T4/T3, nonsuppressed TSH, exclusion of assay artifact, and no pituitary tumor strongly supports RTHβ.
objective: Recognize resistance to thyroid hormone beta as a THRB receptor-signaling defect that causes elevated free thyroid hormones with inappropriately nonsuppressed TSH due impaired negative feedback.
clues: elevated free T4 and T3 on repeat testing
